title: Bundle Size, Tree Shaking & Code Splitting
objectives: Explain what the browser pays for every kilobyte of JavaScript
Write module patterns that tree shaking can actually remove
Split code by route with dynamic imports in Vue Router
Measure bundle cost and initial-load coverage before and after
body:
Every kilobyte of JavaScript costs three times: download, parse/compile, and execute on the main thread. CSS and images can be streamed and rendered progressively; JavaScript must be fully parsed and run before it does anything. The fastest request is the one you never make, and the fastest code is the code you never ship.

## The problem
Your app imports a utility library, a date library and an icon set through one big barrel file (`index.js` that re-exports everything). The bundle is 1.1 MB although you use maybe 15% of it, and first paint waits for all of it.

## Constraints
- Tree shaking only removes exports the bundler can prove are unused, which requires ES module `import`/`export` syntax.
- A module with side effects (top-level code that runs, polyfills, CSS injections) cannot be dropped safely unless you declare otherwise.
- Route-level splitting helps only if the router actually lazy-loads route components.
- Gzip/Brotli sizes are what the network pays, but parse/execute cost scales closer to the raw size.

## Options
Three levers, in the order you should pull them:

```js
// 1. Shakeable imports: named ESM imports, no barrel re-export-all
import { debounce } from "lodash-es"          // only debounce is bundled
import format from "date-fns/format"          // per-module path, very shakeable

// 2. Route-level splitting: each page becomes its own chunk
const routes = [
  { path: "/", component: Home },                     // eager: landing must be fast
  { path: "/admin", component: () => import("./views/AdminView.vue") }
]

// 3. On-demand feature loading, after first paint
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const { openEditor } = await import("./editor.js")  // fetched on first use
  openEditor()
})
```

## Tradeoffs
Splitting shrinks the initial bundle but creates request waterfalls: if a lazy route triggers another import, the user waits through a chain of round trips. Too many tiny chunks waste bytes on HTTP overhead; one giant chunk wastes bytes on code the user never opens. Aggressive `sideEffects: false` declarations can silently break modules that do have side effects.

## Decision
Ship one eager chunk with the shell (app frame, router, state, landing view) and split everything behind navigation. Prefer per-module imports for big libraries. Add `/* webpackPrefetch: true */`-style hints or `<link rel=prefetch>` only for routes users hit most of the time.

## Measure it
Run the build with a bundle analyzer and record: total size, initial (eager) chunk size, all in both raw and Brotli bytes. In DevTools → Coverage, load the app and read how much shipped JavaScript actually executed. After each change, rebuild and compare the same three numbers — a split that does not shrink the initial chunk is noise.

## Best practices
- Import big libraries with named ESM imports or per-module paths.
- Lazy-load every route component except the landing one.
- Mark true side-effect-free packages with `sideEffects: false` in package.json.
- Review bundle size diffs in code review, not after production complaints.
- Budget the initial chunk (e.g. under 200 KB Brotli) and enforce it in CI.

## Common mistakes
- Re-exporting everything from a barrel file, which defeats tree shaking analysis.
- Dynamic-importing components that the landing page needs anyway, adding a waterfall to first paint.
- Celebrating a smaller raw bundle while measuring nothing about parse/execute time.
- Splitting so finely that navigation waits on three sequential chunk requests.
- Treating minified+Brotli size as the only number; execution cost follows the raw size.

exercise.prompt: Compute the initial bundle cost. Each module reports its size in KB and whether it is imported statically (part of the initial chunk) or dynamically (lazy chunk). Render the initial total and the lazy total, and per module whether it blocks first load. The initial-sum logic has a bug: it counts every module.
hints: inInitial must return true only for import === "static".
initialKb should filter with inInitial before summing, exactly like lazyKb does.
After the fix, initial should be 112 KB and lazy 450 KB.

questions.prompt: Which import pattern is most tree-shakeable?
options: import * as utils from "./utils-index.js" where the barrel re-exports everything
questions.explanation: A named import from an ES module lets the bundler keep only the referenced export; barrel files and CommonJS whole-package imports pull in code the analyzer cannot prove unused.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of splitting code into very many tiny chunks?
options: Navigation can become a waterfall of sequential small requests with HTTP overhead
The main thread can no longer parse the chunks
Brotli refuses to compress files under 10 KB
questions.explanation: Over-splitting trades one big download for many round trips; if chunk B needs chunk A first, users wait through the chain.
